objectives.label: Put the centaur markers back up
Helped the Bracken family get home
Shared supper with the cinder wolves

facet_ford.name: The Ford Stone
facet_ford.text: Wrapped in a witch's wool sock. It rings every bell charm it passes, and won't stop.

charm_ford_witch.name: Mother Thrum's Tuned Charm
charm_ford_witch.text: A bell charm tuned to the note the stones hum. Hold it near a gem and it sings.

scene_parade.narration: The shortest road north is a parade: gem wagons up to their axles in ruts, a campfire on every rise, and centaur relay-runners weaving through it all at a canter. Then the whole parade stops. Somebody up ahead is shouting "NUMBERS! GET YOUR NUMBERS!"

choices.label: Walk up to the front and see why
Read the crowd like a book
Sniff the gem wagons

scene_parade_sniff_wagons.narration: Your dragonling sniffs the nearest gem wagon and goes very still. It smells of home: warm rock, ash, the inside of a cave. And underneath that, a hum you can feel in your teeth. Every wagon in the parade smells the same, all the way to the front.

choices.label: Walk on up the column

scene_parade_read_crowd.narration: Your kitsune reads the queue the way other people read a menu. That wagon is two places ahead of where it should be. That man is selling the same pebble twice. Those three are a family and that one only says she is. By the time you are halfway up the column, you know the whole queue's business, and the queue does not know you know.

choices.label: Walk on up the column

scene_spilled_pannier.narration: Halfway up the column, a gem wagon drops a wheel into a rut, and a pannier splits open. Little gem chips pour into the road like spilled sweets. Every head turns. The drover on the box is the lead drover, the boss of the whole river crossing up ahead, and he has a voice like a bass drum. "MIND YOUR BOOTS!" he booms. Somebody's dog is already sniffing the chips with great interest.

choices.label: Scoop up the chips before the crowd does
Hold back and watch the scramble
Spot every last chip, even the ones in the mud

check_catch_chips.prompt: Scoop up rolling gem chips before the crowd does

onSuccess.narration: You dive, scoop and pass, scoop and pass, and every chip is back in the pannier before a single pocket gets one. The drover counts them twice, then booms a thank you so loud the horses jump. He will remember your faces.

onFailure.narration: You scoop up a whole double handful, very proudly, and give the drover three chips and a great deal of gravel. He laughs so hard his hat falls off. By the time he finds it, the crowd has pocketed the rest.

scene_spilled_pannier_hold_back.narration: You stand back. The crowd scrambles, squabbles and stuffs its pockets. Nobody notices what you notice: every chip in the dust is humming, very faintly, like a kettle a long way off. When the last chip is gone, the road goes quiet, and so does the hum.

choices.label: Walk on to the front

scene_spilled_pannier_spot_all.narration: Your bigfoot stops, looks once, and points. Under the wheel. In a hoofprint. Inside somebody's boot. Every chip goes back in the pannier, even the one the dog was guarding. The drover stares. "Never seen eyes like that," he booms. "I'll remember you lot."

choices.label: Walk on to the front

scene_number_pebble.narration: The road ends at the west branch of the river, and the queue to cross it is two days long. A faun provisioner named Burdock is selling numbered pebbles out of a bucket, and honeycakes at bridge-queue prices, which means three times what they are worth. Your pebble says 412. The ford is on number 9.

choices.label: Buy a very expensive honeycake
Pocket your pebble and look around

scene_number_pebble_buy_cake.narration: Burdock sells you a honeycake the size of a coin for the price of a honeycake the size of a hat. "My lucky number," he says fondly, and means your money. It is, to be fair, a very good honeycake. You make it last three bites.

choices.label: Look around the camp

scene_number_pebble_pocket_pebble.narration: You pocket pebble 412 and keep your coins. Burdock does not mind a bit. "Plenty of time to get hungry, my lucky numbers," he says. "Two whole days of it." He goes back to shouting, and his goat, Pudding, goes back to staring at the pebble bucket with great interest.

choices.label: Look around the camp

choice_runaway_goat.narration: CRASH. Burdock's goat, Pudding, has knocked over the pebble bucket and is galloping down the queue with it stuck on her head. Numbers fly everywhere. Two hundred people start arguing at once about who was number 37. "My bucket!" wails Burdock. "My numbers! My GOAT!" Everybody vote.

choices.label: Chase Pudding down the queue
Help sort the numbers back into the bucket
Tempt Pudding with a crumb of honeycake

check_goat_chase.prompt: Catch a goat with a bucket on her head

onSuccess.narration: You zig when Pudding zigs and zag when she zags, and grab the bucket by its handle just as she leaps a cooking pot. Pudding thinks this was a wonderful game. For the rest of the day, wherever you go, a goat goes too.

onFailure.narration: Pudding leaps a cooking pot, a sleeping drover and a small tent. You leap the cooking pot, mostly. In the end she trots back to Burdock all by herself, very pleased, with the bucket still on her head.

choice_runaway_goat_sort.narration: You crawl about picking up pebbles and asking everybody, very fairly, what number they had. It takes ages. Most people tell the truth. Burdock is so grateful that he gives you a honeycake for free, which he says has never happened before and must never be mentioned.

choices.label: Dust off your knees

choice_runaway_goat_crumb.narration: You hold out one crumb of honeycake. Pudding stops dead, drops the bucket, and eats the crumb very delicately off your palm. Then she gazes at you with her strange goat eyes, as if you are the most important person in the world. For the rest of the day, wherever you go, a goat goes too.

choices.label: Walk on, with a goat

scene_three_cards.narration: Behind Burdock's stall, a kitsune in a tall hat is shuffling three cards on an upturned barrel. "Find the Sun Card, win a front-of-the-queue pebble!" Nobody ever finds the Sun Card. Her tails keep twitching every time she shuffles.

choices.label: Watch her tails and catch the trick
Wink at her, one fox to another
Offer to help her draw a crowd
Keep your coins and walk on by

check_expose.prompt: Spot where the Sun Card really goes

onSuccess.narration: Every time she shuffles, the third tail flicks the Sun Card up her sleeve. You say so, loudly and politely.

onFailure.narration: You pick the middle card with total confidence. It is a picture of a very smug fox. The crowd laughs, and so, to be fair, does she.

scene_exposed.narration: The kitsune, whose name turns out to be Tamsin Three-Cards, sighs and shakes the Sun Card out of her sleeve. The whole crowd gets their pebbles back. The drovers at the front of the queue have noticed you, and drovers remember faces.

choices.label: Head for the smell of soup

scene_join_con.narration: You stand in the crowd and gasp very loudly every time somebody almost wins. Tamsin pays you with a front-of-the-queue pebble and a wink. It is shiny and it says number 1, and it is absolutely not fair.

choices.label: Head for the smell of soup

scene_three_cards_walk_by.narration: You keep your coins in your pocket and walk on by. Tamsin tips her tall hat to you anyway. "Smart ones," she says. "Come back when you feel lucky. Nobody ever is, but come back." Behind you, somebody loses again, very loudly.

choices.label: Head for the smell of soup

scene_soup_line.narration: At the edge of camp, people in dark robes with little crystals on strings are giving away soup to anyone whose season has gone wrong. A cheerful ladler named Wend fills your bowls without asking a single question. "Kindness first," says Wend. "Always." The crystal on Wend's string is humming, very faintly.

choices.label: Say thank you and eat up
Ask why the crystal is humming

scene_soup_line_ask_crystal.narration: Wend lifts the crystal and looks at it as if it has only just started. "It's done that since the red night," Wend says. "Whenever a gem wagon passes. We think it's trying to say something." Wend tucks it back inside the robe, where it goes on humming against Wend's heart.

choices.label: Finish your soup

scene_soup_line_thank_wend.narration: "Thank you," you say. Wend beams and fills your bowls a second time, without asking, and remembers all your names after hearing them once. "Kindness first," says Wend again, as if it is a rule the whole world ought to have. The crystal on the string hums, very faintly, the whole time.

choices.label: Finish your soup

scene_queue_jumpers.narration: Down the line comes a gang in matching red scarves, shoving past everybody. "Ford's closing tomorrow!" they shout. "Let us through, it's urgent!" It is not urgent, and the ford is not closing. An old faun in front of you gets squeezed against a wagon wheel, and his hat gets knocked into the soup.

choices.label: Stand shoulder to shoulder and hold the line
Run and fetch the drovers
Tell them, sweetly, that the back is the new front
Ask Tamsin to keep them busy

check_block_jumpers.prompt: Hold the queue against a shoving gang

onSuccess.narration: You link arms with the old faun and two very surprised strangers, and the red scarves bounce off you like a ball off a wall. They grumble all the way back to the end of the queue. The whole line cheers, and the red scarves will remember you.

onFailure.narration: The red scarves squeeze past, all elbows. Then the last one trips over Pudding's bucket, and the whole gang goes down in a red-scarfed heap. The queue laughs so hard that they slink off to the back anyway.

scene_queue_jumpers_call_drovers.narration: You run down to the ford and fetch the lead drover. He walks back up the queue without hurrying, stands in front of the red scarves, and says one word. "BACK." His voice rattles the wagon wheels. They go back. The drover gives you a slow nod, and fishes the old faun's hat out of the soup.

choices.label: Back to your place in line

scene_queue_jumpers_send_back.narration: Your kitsune smiles the sweetest smile in the queue. "Oh, haven't you heard? The ford moved. The back is the front now." The red scarves look at each other and then sprint, very fast, all the way to the back. It takes them an hour to work it out. By then they are too embarrassed to come back.

choices.label: Back to your place in line

scene_queue_jumpers_tamsin_help.narration: Tamsin strolls up shuffling her cards. "Find the Sun Card, win a place at the front!" The red scarves crowd round to play. They play for an hour. They never find the Sun Card. By the time they give up, the queue has rolled on without them, and Tamsin gives you a wink.

choices.label: Back to your place in line

scene_relay_message.narration: A centaur relay-runner skids to a stop beside you, talking before she has even stopped. "Message for the drovers at the ford, can't go myself, got the hill road next, you look fast, or loud, or both." She presses a rolled-up note into your hands. It says: RIVER RISING. CROSS SLOW.

choices.label: Run the note down to the ford
Sing it down the queue, the relay way
Fly the note straight to the ford

check_run_message.prompt: Run a message down a two-day queue

onSuccess.narration: You weave through wagons, goats and campfires, and slap the note into the lead drover's hand. He reads it, nods, and slows the crossing to a careful walk. When you get back, the runner tosses you a brave whistle. "The relay remembers," she says.

onFailure.narration: You run as fast as you can and hand the note to the wrong drover, who reads it out loud to absolutely everybody. That, it turns out, works just as well. By lunchtime the whole queue knows the river is rising.

scene_relay_message_sing.narration: The runner shows you the relay way: you do not carry a message, you sing it. You sing RIVER RISING, CROSS SLOW to the next campfire, and they sing it to the next, and it rolls down the queue like a wave. By the time it reaches the ford, it has a tune and a chorus, and somebody is clapping.

choices.label: Listen to it roll away

scene_relay_message_fly.narration: Your griffin takes the note in a beak and is over the whole queue in four wingbeats. The lead drover reads it, looks up at the river, and nods. When you land back beside the runner, she whistles. "The relay could use a friend with wings," she says, and gallops off before you can answer.

choices.label: Land back in the queue

choice_tolls.narration: Two days is a long time to stand in a line, and the rush is charging its own tolls. A wagon is stuck to its axles in mud. A centaur marker line has been knocked flat by queue-jumpers. And a faun family called the Brackens is sitting beside a cracked cart wheel, very quiet. Everybody vote.

choices.label: Un-mire the stuck wagon
Put the centaur markers back up
Fly the marker line and spot every post
Sit down with the Brackens

check_unmire.prompt: Heave a gem wagon out of the mud

onSuccess.narration: One, two, THREE, and the wagon comes out with a noise like a giant boot leaving a puddle. The drover gives you a brave whistle and calls you "mudlarks", which is a compliment.

onFailure.narration: The wagon comes out in the end, but only after everyone has sat down in the mud at least once. You will be finding mud in your ears until next week.

check_markers.prompt: Put the markers back in the right order

onSuccess.narration: Post by post, you walk the line back into order, reading the worn numbers with your thumbs where the paint has gone. The last marker goes in with a thump, and the whole line points, straight and plain, at the one safe way down to the ford.

onFailure.narration: You put them all back up, beautifully, in the wrong order. A centaur runner gallops past, stops, laughs, and fixes them in about four seconds.

scene_markers_restored.narration: The marker line stands straight again, every post pointing the safe way to the ford. A centaur relay-runner slows down just long enough to say "The relay remembers," and then she is gone, already singing it to the next runner up the road.

choices.label: Back to camp before dusk

scene_family.narration: The Brackens' cart wheel is cracked, their season is over, and they need to get home before the river rises. The littlest Bracken is holding a queue pebble with a big number on it and trying very hard not to cry about it.

choices.label: Swap pebbles, so they cross before you
Share your honeycake
Lash the wheel together with rope

scene_family_fix_wheel.narration: You lash the cracked wheel together with rope, round and round, until it looks like a wheel wearing a jumper. It turns. It wobbles, but it turns. The littlest Bracken rides on top of the cart to test it and declares it the best wheel ever made, which is not true, but it will get them home.

choices.label: Back to camp before dark

scene_family_share_cake.narration: You break the honeycake into four, then five, so the littlest Bracken gets a bit from everyone. For a while nobody says anything, because honeycake. Then the mother says their season was not all bad, really, and the littlest one falls asleep against a cart wheel with crumbs on both cheeks.

choices.label: Back to camp before dark

scene_family_give_pebble.narration: You hand the littlest Bracken your pebble, and take theirs. Their number is enormous. Yours was not. The littlest Bracken looks at the small number for a long time and then stops trying not to cry and just cries, happily, all over it. The Brackens will cross at dawn, and they do not stop thanking you until dusk.

choices.label: Back to camp before dark

scene_dusk_wolves.narration: At dusk, cinder wolves come and sit just past the firelight, cold and thin, with a faint warm glow under their fur. They are not hunting. They are pointedly not sitting anywhere near the gem wagons. Every campfire in the queue is arguing about whether to feed them.

choices.label: Share your supper with them
Leave them be and keep your fire small
Shoo them away from the camp

scene_wolves_fed.narration: You put your supper down on a flat stone and step back. The wolves eat politely, and then the whole pack lies down in a heap by your fire, glowing like a pile of coals. It is the warmest night anybody in the queue has had all week. The road will remember this.

choices.label: Follow the laughter to the big campfire

scene_dusk_wolves_leave_be.narration: You keep your fire small and your voices low. The wolves stay just past the light all evening, watching. Not you. The gem wagons. Every time a wagon creaks, every ear goes flat, and the pack shuffles a little farther away from it. Whatever they are worried about, it is not you.

choices.label: Follow the laughter to the big campfire

encounter_wolves.narration: The wolves do not want to leave. They are cold, and your fire is right there.

onVictory.narration: The pack slinks off down the queue to the next fire, where somebody feeds them. The whole campsite hears about who shooed and who shared.

onDefeat.narration: The wolves win the argument, eat everybody's supper, and curl up on your bedrolls. There will be no sleeping there tonight, so you wander off, cold and hungry, toward the laughter at the big campfire.

scene_campfire_play.narration: Round the biggest campfire, a troupe of rush folk is acting out the red night with blankets and saucepans: the mountain, the red sky, the stones falling like rain. It is a big hit. Then their mountain gets the hiccups. "We need a new mountain, darlings!" cries the troupe leader, and stares straight at you.

choices.label: Volunteer to play the mountain
Tell them what you really heard: the humming
Let Pudding play the mountain
Take over the play and give it a better ending

check_play_mountain.prompt: Be a mountain in front of the whole camp

onSuccess.narration: You stand on a barrel under a red blanket and RUMBLE. You erupt with a sack of pinecones. Three small children shriek with joy. The troupe leader says you are the best mountain they have ever had, and pays you a honeycake in wages.

onFailure.narration: You stand on a barrel under a red blanket, take an enormous breath to rumble, and sneeze instead. The blanket flies off. Everybody agrees it is the most surprising eruption yet, and the troupe keeps the sneeze in the show.

scene_campfire_play_tell_true.narration: You tell the campfire what you really heard: not a bang, but a hum, in every gem on the road. The troupe goes quiet. Somebody takes a gem out of a pocket and holds it to an ear. Then somebody else does. Soon the whole campfire sits very still, listening to their pockets humming one quiet note.

choices.label: Walk on down the queue

scene_campfire_play_goat_mountain.narration: Pudding climbs onto the barrel, wears the red blanket, and eats the script. Then she bleats, once, with tremendous feeling. The crowd goes wild. It is the finest eruption the troupe has ever staged, and Pudding takes three bows, all of them by accident.

choices.label: Walk on down the queue

scene_campfire_play_rewrite.narration: Your kitsune reads the audience and changes the play on the spot. In the new ending, the stones are not treasure at all. They are a puzzle, and everyone in the play sets off to find out what the puzzle is. The crowd likes it better. The troupe leader writes it down, muttering, "Better. Annoyingly better."

choices.label: Walk on down the queue

scene_witch_stall.narration: Farther down the queue there is a remedy stall with a pointed hat hanging off the corner. Every time a gem wagon rolls past, all the little bell charms on the stall ring by themselves, and the witch behind the counter winces. Her name is Mother Thrum. She looks at you over her spectacles. "What do you actually want?"

choices.label: Ask her a real question: why are the charms ringing?
Ask for something for sore feet

scene_witch_stall_sore_feet.narration: Mother Thrum hands you a sunbloom draught without looking, because sore feet are the one thing everybody in a queue wants. Then she looks. "That's a want," she says. "It isn't the want." She raises one eyebrow and waits to see if you have a better question.

choices.label: Ask a better question

scene_tuned_charm.narration: "Better question than most," says Mother Thrum, and she hands you one bell charm she has tuned to the note the stones are humming. Hold it near a gem and it sings. The note is older than the road, she says, and the centaurs will tell you the road was here before everything. On her shelf, wrapped in a thick wool sock, is a stone that will not stop ringing.

choices.label: Answer her question, truly
Tell her where it fell from, and promise to take it home
Leave the stone in its sock

scene_tuned_charm_leave_it.narration: You leave the stone in its sock on her shelf. Mother Thrum nods, not surprised, and tucks the wool tighter round it. "Then it rings another night," she says. "And so do I." The charms on the stall all chime once, softly, as a wagon rolls past in the dark.

choices.label: Walk back to your fire

scene_tuned_charm_take_it_home.narration: You tell her where it fell from, and that you mean to take it back. Mother Thrum unwraps the sock. The ringing stops the moment the stone touches your dragonling's hands, as if it has recognized the smell of home. "There," she says softly. "It knows." She gives you the sock as well. "Keep it warm."

choices.label: Walk back to your fire

check_answer.prompt: Tell Mother Thrum what you actually want, and mean it

onSuccess.narration: Mother Thrum listens all the way to the end, then hands you the sock with the stone in it. "That's the Ford Stone. Take it somewhere it stops ringing," she says. "I'd like some sleep."

onFailure.narration: You say something about gems and glory, and Mother Thrum's charms all go quiet at once, which feels like an answer. "Not yet," she says kindly. "Ask yourself again at the mountain."

scene_charm_walk.narration: Walking back to your fire in the dark, the tuned charm will not keep quiet. It sings at every gem wagon you pass. "Listen with it," Mother Thrum told you. "Then work out what you heard." The queue is asleep, mostly. Where do you hold it up?

choices.label: Hold it to the gem wagons, one after another
Hold it out toward the cinder wolves
Hold it right up against the Ford Stone

check_listen_charm.prompt: Listen for what changes from wagon to wagon

onSuccess.narration: Wagon after wagon, gem after gem, and the note never changes. Not higher. Not lower. Big gems and tiny chips all sing the very same note, as if they all came from one place. One very, very old place.

onFailure.narration: So many wagons, so much singing, that the notes blur together in your head like a choir with a cold. You will have to listen again somewhere quieter. Still, you are sure of one thing: every gem is singing.

scene_charm_walk_wolves.narration: You hold the charm out into the dark where the wolves are lying. It sings. Every wolf flattens its ears, gets up, and moves ten steps farther off, politely, like guests leaving a party early. They are not afraid of you. They are keeping away from the note.

choices.label: Settle in for the night

scene_charm_walk_ford_stone.narration: You hold the charm against the wool sock. The charm and the stone ring together, exactly together, so loudly that every bell in the queue answers. Sleepy people sit up and say "WHAT?" Then both go quiet at the very same moment, as if they had finished saying something to each other.

choices.label: Settle in for the night

rest_witch_fire.narration: You sleep in the queue with three hundred strangers, a lot of snoring, and Pudding, who wanders from fire to fire all night, eating anything left out. The little tuned charm chimes softly every time a gem wagon creaks past in the dark. Queues move at night, it turns out, because drovers never sleep. In the morning, Burdock comes to fetch Pudding home for her breakfast, and she trots off after him, very pleased with herself. A drover is shouting numbers, and the ford is a great deal closer than it was.

choices.label: Go down to the water at dawn

scene_crossing_verse.narration: At dawn the lead drover stands at the water's edge, singing the crossing verse, one line for every step: slow, and slow, and wait, and slow. "Anybody who crosses my ford," he booms, "crosses at the verse's pace." The river is higher than yesterday. The relay's message was right.

choices.label: Learn the crossing verse, line by line
Watch the water instead of the singer
Let the drover who knows you teach you

check_learn_verse.prompt: Learn a drover song well enough to cross by it

onSuccess.narration: You hum along under your breath, then a little louder, and by the third time through you are singing it with him. The drover's eyebrows go up. "Huh," he booms. "You've got it." The verse sits in your chest like a steady drum.

onFailure.narration: You learn a verse beautifully, with feeling. It turns out to be the one about turnips that the drovers sing at supper. The drover is far too pleased to tell you until much later.

scene_crossing_verse_watch.narration: You watch the river instead. In the middle, the current runs smooth and slow. But near the west edge it pulls hard and fast, off toward the green smudge of the marsh. Anything that slips in there will go west, and keep going west. You make a note: stay away from the west edge.

choices.label: Go down to the ford

scene_crossing_verse_drover_teaches.narration: The lead drover spots you and crooks a finger. "You lot. Here." He sings each line once, slowly, and makes you sing it back until it is right. "Now you know it," he booms, "and now the river knows you know it." Then he calls you mudlarks, which is what he calls everybody he likes.

choices.label: Go down to the ford

choice_ford.narration: The ford is wide and brown and fast. The drovers cross with ceremony: one wagon at a time, slow and steady, while the lead drover sings the crossing verse. Behind you, the whole queue is watching.

choices.label: Cross with the caravans, at the drovers' pace
Sing the crossing verse with every step
The drovers you helped wave you in beside the lead wagon
Follow the marker line you put back up
Ride across on the Brackens' cart
Use Tamsin's front-of-the-queue pebble

check_ford.prompt: Keep your footing in the ford

onSuccess.narration: Step, wait, step. The water pushes and pulls and you do not let it. The lead drover sings the last line of the verse just as your boots hit the north bank.

onFailure.narration: Halfway across, somebody behind you shouts, and then everybody behind you shouts, and the water that was pushing at your knees is suddenly pushing at your waist.

onSuccess.narration: With friends on every side, the ford is just very wet walking. Somebody up on a wagon starts clapping as you reach the north bank.

onFailure.narration: You are nearly across, with friends on every side, when a yell goes up behind you and the whole river seems to lurch at once.

scene_surge.narration: Halfway across, the red-scarf queue-jumpers charge into the water behind you, and a wagon full of bread tips over with a SPLASH. Two river drakes surface at once, very interested in the bread. The current is shoving at your knees.

choices.label: Toss the drakes their toll: the floating bread
Hold the wagon up, whatever the drakes think
Shout at the red scarves to grab the wagon
Let go and ride the current

check_drake_toll.prompt: Pay the river drakes politely in bread

onSuccess.narration: The drakes take the bread like a toll collector takes coins, and one of them even nudges the wagon back onto its wheels with its nose. Drovers haul you up the north bank by your collars.

onFailure.narration: One drake takes the bread. The other one wanted the bread you were holding, and it bumps you, very gently, into the deep part.

encounter_drakes.narration: The drakes do not see why a wagon full of bread should stay upright when it could be lunch.

onVictory.narration: The drakes sulk off downstream with one loaf each, and the drovers cheer as you shove the wagon up onto the north bank.

onDefeat.narration: A drake flicks its tail, the wagon goes over, and you go with it, bread and bags and all, off into the current.

scene_surge_scarves_help.narration: "YOU LOT!" you shout. The red scarves stare. Then their leader shrugs. "Fair's fair," she says, and the whole gang wades in and grabs the wagon. Together you heave it upright while the drakes squabble over the bread. Everybody staggers up the north bank, soaked to the ears, and the red scarves even say sorry.

choices.label: Climb out on the north bank

end_forded.narration: You stand dripping on the north bank of the west branch, with the whole rush pouring past you toward the mountain. The tuned charm in your pocket is still chiming at every wagon. Behind you, the crossing verse starts again for the next wagon in line. Tonight you camp on the north side, warm and loud and very much in the thick of it.

end_marsh_west.narration: The west branch does what rivers do: it whooshes you west into the green tangles of the Whispering Marsh, past a boggart in a reed hat who applauds. At last the channels let you go on a muddy bank near MossHome, at the flooded edge of the Enchanted Woods. You never chose this road, but here you are, and the tuned charm is still humming. The road people will hear about it. The road people hear about everything.

end_swept_setback.narration: The current takes you a long, long way west, through the marsh's tangles and out the far side, three days later than you meant to arrive anywhere. You wash up on the flooded paths of the Enchanted Woods with wet bags, a cold supper, and a drake-shaped grudge. It is not the road you chose, and it cost you time, but you made it out and the charm is still humming.

voiceGuide.tone: busy, loud, funny road-camp country; warm underneath, a little spooky at dusk, never scary

npcVoices.burdock: a faun provisioner; cheerful, shameless about his prices, calls everyone 'my lucky number'; owns Pudding, a goat with a weakness for buckets
npcVoices.tamsin: Tamsin Three-Cards, a kitsune card-sharp; quick, delighted to be caught, never sore about losing
npcVoices.wend: a Deep Hollow soup ladler; gentle, generous, asks nothing, says 'kindness first' and means it a little too much
npcVoices.mother_thrum: a ford witch; careful and instructive, peers over spectacles, always asks 'what do you actually want?'
npcVoices.drover: the lead drover; slow, booming voice, sings the crossing verse and will not be hurried
npcVoices.relay_runner: a centaur relay-runner; talks while galloping, never finishes a sentence in the same place she started it
npcVoices.brackens: the Brackens, a faun family whose season is over; tired, polite, the littlest one very brave about it
npcVoices.troupe_leader: a rush-camp actor-manager; grand and dramatic, calls everyone 'darlings', thrilled by any eruption
npcVoices.red_scarves: the red-scarf queue-jumpers' leader; pushy and impatient, but fair when fairly beaten
